messages.author: b24eeb356a7b40a5
messages.subject: Questions about intercept
parts:
Hello everyone,

I'm currently in the process of learning SEM and I have a few questions that I can't seem to solve.
I'm trying to build a very simple model where I want to measure a latent variable "literacy" made up of 5 observed variables, with the code provided (both outputs are attached) :

model_lit <- '
  # measurement model
  litterratie =~ lit_form_medn + lit_suivre_instn + lit_lire_santen + lit_lire_medocn + lit_comprendre_prof_santen
'
# First model
fit.sem_lit1.1 <- sem(model_lit, data = dat_sem)
summary(fit.sem_lit1.1, standardized=TRUE)

# Second model
fit.sem_lit1.2 <- sem(model_lit, data = dat_sem, meanstructure = TRUE)
summary(fit.sem_lit1.2, standardized=TRUE)

My question is as follows: why, in a model where I don't specify to estimate the intercepts, 1) do I obtain exactly the same parameter and variance estimates as when I specify that I want to estimate the intercepts, 2) does the number of free parameters increase from 10 to 15 without decreasing the degrees of freedom of the chi-square test?
So, are intercepts not estimated by default by the cfa or sem functions?

I hope my question is clear, and I sincerely thank you for any answer or insight you'll provide.

Best,
Erwan

messages.author: 38226bd700051927
messages.subject: Re: Questions about intercept
parts:
Dear Erwan,

For 1), I don't know how to give you an exact technical explanation, but more or less I would say that the estimation of the covariance structure is independent of the estimation of the mean structure.

For 2), you are increasing the number of parameter estimates by 5 (the 5 intercepts), but you are also increasing the number of "data points" you use to estimate the model, by using the (5) means of your observable variables. You can run the computations like this:

Without mean structure:
Nº of data values: 5 variances + 10 covariances = 15
Nº of parameters: 4 loadings + 5 unique variances + 1 latent variance = 10
DoF: 15 - 10 = 5

With mean structure:
Nº of data values: 5 variances + 10 covariances + 5 means = 20
Nº of parameters: 4 factor loadings + 5 unique variances + 1 latent variance + 5 intercepts = 15
DoF: 20 - 15 = 5

Hope it helps!

--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.
GitHub | ORCID

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Questions about intercept
parts:
Daniel's explanation is entirely correct, but I want to expand just a bit. Part of the issue with fit not changing is that the mean structure model is saturated. You have 5 observed means as data points, and you estimate 5 mean structure parameters, the intercepts. A saturated model does not contribute to lack of fit. Your covariance structure model is not saturated, so if you estimated only mean structure first and then added covariance structure, you would see a change in fit.
     The maximum likelihood discrepancy function for a mean and covariance structure model includes two parts, one part for the covariance structure and one part for the mean structure. There is no interaction term. Few models entangle the two together, although ones that do so, ironically, are latent interaction models. One could also imagine some multiple group analyses creating the potential for the two parts of the model to interact, such that certain forms of misspecification of mean structure might lead to bias in estimation of some covariance structure parameters.
     I believe the lavaan package functions do not automatically estimate mean structure parameters unless your model syntax explicitly mentions a mean structure parameter. But check your output to be sure. Yes, it is unnerving when the number of parameters estimated changes but degrees of freedom do not. Maybe the software needs to break down parameters estimated and degrees of freedom by mean structure vs covariance structure.

messages.author: 0325c6a976085eab
messages.subject: Re: Questions about intercept
parts:
A lot of the time we're not very interested in the intercepts in SEM, so unless you actually say you are interested in them, lavaan doesn't bother to show them to you.

Every time you add some data to your model ( a mean, variance or covariance) you gain a degree of freedom. And every time you add a parameter to your model, it costs a degree of freedom.

So when you say you want to estimate intercepts, you add6 more pieces of data (the means of the six variables) to your model. Then you say that you want to estimate six things (the intercepts) so we are back where we started.

The six intercepts don't change anything, that part of the model is saturated - so it won't have any effect on the rest of the model.

(Similarly, if you do a regression in lavaan , the predictors are correlated, but these correlations aren't part of the model and might not be reported [depending which function you use to estimate the model]). There's debate about whether you should consider these correlations when calculating the null model.

Hope that helps,

Jeremy
